Abstract This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) implementation, perceptions of public services, and trust in government on citizen satisfaction within the Abu Dhabi Police, offering insights into the role of emerging technologies in public administration. Guided by Public Value Theory, Expectation-Confirmation Theory, and IT Assimilation Theory, the research develops a conceptual framework to examine both direct and mediated relationships among these constructs. A purposive sample of 500 police employees from AI-enabled, operational, and administrative units was surveyed using a structured questionnaire, from which 365 valid responses were analyzed to assess the relationships among AI implementation, perception of public services, trust in government, and citizen satisfaction. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS, enabling a robust assessment of the measurement and structural models. The findings reveal that AI implementation significantly enhances citizens’ satisfaction, particularly when services are transparent, efficient, and aligned with public expectations. Perceptions of public service quality also emerged as a critical determinant of satisfaction, reflecting the importance of accessibility, responsiveness, and fairness in shaping positive citizen experiences. Trust in government was found to play a crucial mediating role, strengthening the link between AI-enabled services, public service perceptions, and satisfaction outcomes. Importantly, the results indicate partial mediation, suggesting that while AI and service quality directly influence satisfaction, their effects are amplified when mediated by trust. These findings highlight the dual importance of technological advancement and institutional credibility in fostering citizen satisfaction. The study contributes theoretically by integrating three complementary frameworks to explain how AI influences service outcomes, and practically by providing evidence-based recommendations for policymakers, AI developers, and law enforcement agencies. Emphasizing transparency, accountability, and ethical AI use can further enhance public trust and maximize satisfaction. This research aligns with the UAE’s Vision 2031 of positioning the nation as a global leader in safety, innovation, and smart governance, while also offering a model for other countries seeking to integrate AI into public service delivery. Introduction In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern governance, particularly in law enforcement, where it is reshaping operational practices and community relations (Shafee et al., 2025). AI-driven tools such as facial recognition, predictive analytics, and real-time surveillance systems are enabling a shift toward “smart policing,” offering enhanced precision in crime detection and prevention (McDaniel & Pease, 2021; Brayne & Christin, 2021). These technologies not only improve the efficacy and responsiveness of police operations but also contribute to the broader goals of safety, transparency, and service efficiency in urban environments (Laufs & Borrion, 2022; Mantri, 2023). The United Arab Emirates (UAE), in alignment with its national Vision 2031, has positioned itself at the forefront of AI adoption across public service domains, including policing (Alghafli, 2021). Since the launch of its national AI strategy in 2017, the UAE has actively integrated AI systems to optimize public safety and increase citizen satisfaction (Almarzooqi, 2019; Radu, 2021). Local governments, particularly Abu Dhabi, have served as innovation hubs, implementing AI technologies that support the country’s ambition to become a global leader in technological governance (Schilirò, 2021). Despite its optimistic potential, AI implementation in policing presents complex challenges. These include public trust, data privacy, and perceptions of fairness (Kreps et al., 2023; Ardabili et al., 2024). Public confidence in law enforcement not only influences the legitimacy of institutions but also affects civic cooperation and engagement (Davies & Krame, 2023; Alshehhi et al., 2024). While AI can improve efficiency and responsiveness, its opaque decision-making processes, often referred to as the “black box” phenomenon, may provoke skepticism and fear among citizens (Bagaric et al., 2022). These concerns are exacerbated when citizens lack clarity about how AI systems operate or are unsure whether such systems reflect community values and human oversight (Agrawal, 2024). In this context, trust becomes not just a passive outcome but also a necessary enabler for AI-driven public service adoption. Simultaneously, the perception of public service quality plays a vital role in shaping satisfaction. Research indicates that citizens are more likely to express approval of government initiatives when services are perceived as accessible, fair, and responsive (Dan, 2020; O'Regan et al., 2022). In the UAE, although public services have seen significant digital enhancements, inconsistencies in delivery, limited transparency in AI operations, and perceived biases continue to hinder citizen confidence (Ekaabi et al., 2020; Kulal et al., 2024). Such perception gaps raise important questions about the extent to which AI can meaningfully improve public satisfaction, particularly when deployed without adequate attention to ethical and communicative standards (Bagaric et al., 2022; Döring, 2022). Moreover, public trust is especially critical in technologically advanced governance contexts such as the UAE, where the government's legitimacy and strategic direction rely heavily on the societal acceptance of innovation (Lockey et al., 2021; Yigitcanlar et al., 2023). While some studies suggest that digital services can enhance trust when implemented transparently (Evans et al., 2021; Alsarraf et al., 2022), others highlight concerns about deepening inequalities due to digital divides and opaque technology governance (El-Haddadeh et al., 2019; Eom & Lee, 2022). Notably, findings remain inconsistent on whether improved service delivery necessarily translates into greater trust, with calls for further investigation into the role of trust in government (Gracia & Arino, 2015; Santa et al., 2019; Li & Shang, 2023). Despite an expanding global body of research exploring the role of AI in public service delivery, significant empirical gaps persist, particularly within the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region and the UAE. Internationally, numerous studies have investigated AI integration into public administration, healthcare, and municipal governance (e.g., Wirtz et al., 2019; Hooda et al., 2022), demonstrating positive outcomes in terms of service efficiency, citizen interaction, and institutional responsiveness. However, the transferability of these insights to the GCC (especially to sectors such as law enforcement and justice) remains underexamined. Specifically, there is a marked lack of empirical studies that assess the direct impact of AI implementation on citizen satisfaction in policing contexts across the GCC, including countries such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. A recent regional review by Kulal et al. (2024) indicated that fewer than five peer-reviewed studies have empirically evaluated AI effects within Middle Eastern police departments and that most of these studies are either exploratory or narrowly focused on technical deployment rather than public perception or behavioral outcomes. Moreover, while the global literature increasingly acknowledges the mediating role of trust in government in shaping public responses to AI adoption (Alsarraf et al., 2022; Li & Shang, 2023), such relationships have not been thoroughly tested in UAE policing environments. In particular, the intersection between trust, AI-enabled public service perception, and satisfaction remains conceptually acknowledged but empirically underexplored in Gulf-specific contexts. This lack of contextual grounding is critical, especially given the UAE’s ambitious AI-driven governance strategy and its unique sociopolitical dynamics, which differ from those of Western democracies, where much of the foundational literature is derived. Additionally, most existing studies remain largely conceptual or theoretical, offering limited real-world applicability for regions undergoing rapid technological transformation in public safety, such as the UAE. There is little data-driven evidence capturing how citizens in high-surveillance, AI-integrated policing environments interpret service quality, fairness, and responsiveness, which are key variables of satisfaction. Given rising urbanization, growing security concerns, and the state’s heavy investment in AI technologies, these gaps hinder both policy innovation and ethical deployment strategies in UAE law enforcement. Therefore, this study aims to fill these critical gaps by developing and empirically validating a conceptual framework that examines the relationships among AI implementation, the perception of public services, trust in the government, and citizen satisfaction in the Abu Dhabi police context. By integrating public value theory, expectation-confirmation theory, and IT assimilation theory, this study provides a multi theoretical lens to examine how AI technologies contribute to (or detract from) citizen-centric public service delivery. Therefore, the primary aim of this study is to examine the impacts of AI implementation, perceptions of public services, and trust in the government on citizen satisfaction with the Abu Dhabi police. Specifically, this research aims to achieve the following objectives: 1) to examine the influence of AI implementation on citizen satisfaction, 2) to examine the influence of public service perceptions on citizen satisfaction, and 3) to analyze the impact of trust in the government on citizen satisfaction. 2. Literature Review 2.1. Artificial Intelligence Implementation Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central tool in transforming public service delivery, particularly by enhancing efficiency, accuracy, and responsiveness in citizen-facing operations (Ahn & Chen, 2022; Chatterjee et al., 2022). AI technologies (ranging from chatbots and predictive analytics to real-time surveillance and automated traffic systems) are https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Alhefaity et al. (2026) 3 increasingly integrated into public sector institutions worldwide to improve service delivery and public engagement (Al Shamsi & Safei, 2023; Kulal et al., 2024). In the UAE, law enforcement agencies have actively adopted AI to streamline crime prediction, enhance emergency responses, and provide real-time public safety solutions, thereby contributing to increased citizen satisfaction (Zhang et al., 2022; Qin & Li, 2024). Satisfaction outcomes are highly contingent on the alignment between AI functionality and citizens’ needs, including speed, transparency, and fairness (Liang et al., 2019; Guo, 2022). When designed with a citizen-centric approach, AI can foster empowerment through better information access, real-time service updates, and greater transparency in governmental operations (Chatterjee et al., 2022). However, alongside these benefits, governments must contend with critical challenges such as privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, and the opacity of AI decision-making, often referred to as the “black box” problem (Rudin, 2019; Bagaric et al., 2022). Ethical risks, accountability gaps, and fears of surveillance may negatively affect citizens’ perceptions, especially in sectors such as law enforcement, where public trust is paramount (Ingrams et al., 2022). While studies have highlighted AI’s role in fostering innovation and operational efficiency (Kleizen et al., 2023), adoption in the public sector remains hindered by assimilation gaps, knowledge limitations, and sociopolitical challenges (Wirtz et al., 2019; Mikalef et al., 2022). In the UAE, these challenges are addressed within the framework of the UAE Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031, which aims to balance innovation with ethical governance, public trust, and security (Mogielnicki, 2023; Al-Shamsi & Ahmad, 2024). Given the documented benefits and risks of AI, this study empirically tests the impact of AI implementation on citizen satisfaction with public safety services in Abu Dhabi, particularly focusing on how AI influences perceptions of police effectiveness, responsiveness, and service quality (Goh et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022). This study hypothesizes the following: H1: AI implementation significantly affects citizen satisfaction. 2.2. Perception of Public Services The perception of public services (PPS) refers to how citizens subjectively interpret the quality, efficiency, and fairness of government-provided services on the basis of personal experience, societal expectations, and institutional reputation (Mensah, 2020; Teshome et al., 2020). Unlike private sector evaluations, which often hinge on price and choice, public sector perceptions are deeply influenced by broader dimensions such as accessibility, responsiveness, and transparency (Ali et al., 2021; Ki, 2021). Research affirms that these perceptions shape public satisfaction and trust, influencing the social contract between governments and citizens (Carter & Grommon, 2017). In the digital age, perceptions are increasingly shaped by the integration of technologies such as AI and the IoT, which enhance not only service efficiency but also real-time responsiveness and personalization (Wirtz et al., 2018). However, while such technologies offer gains in service delivery, they also raise concerns regarding privacy, equity, and interpretability of AI-driven decisions (Robinson, 2020). In the UAE, AI has been strategically deployed in public policing to improve crime prevention, emergency response, and citizen engagement, transforming the public's interaction with safety institutions (Achanta, 2025; Zuiderwijk et al., 2021). Studies show that when services are perceived as effective, timely, and fair (particularly when enhanced by technologies that citizens understand and trust), their satisfaction with government institutions increases significantly (Liang et al., 2019; Henman, 2020; Chan et al., 2021). Platforms that enable direct, transparent interaction between the police and public, such as mobile apps and online portals, have further shaped these positive perceptions in the UAE context (Almesafri & Habes, 2022). Nevertheless, public perception remains sensitive to concerns around data security, algorithmic bias, and transparency in AI usage (Wirtz et al., 2021; Haley & Burrell, 2025). As a result, governments must balance technological innovation with ethical oversight to ensure that public trust and satisfaction are not compromised. Drawing on expectation-confirmation theory (ECT), which posits that satisfaction arises from alignment between expectations and actual service performance (He & Ma, 2021; Li & Shang, 2023), this study hypothesizes that citizen satisfaction with Abu Dhabi police services is significantly influenced by how these services are perceived, particularly in terms of their efficiency, reliability, and technological integration (Alkraiji & Ameen, 2022; Kulal et al., 2024). H2: The perception of public services significantly affects citizen satisfaction. 2.3. Trust in the government Trust in the government (TG) is broadly defined as the confidence of citizens in the government’s actions to act fairly, competently, and in the public’s best interest (OECD, 2013; Kumagai & Ilorio, 2020). It plays a foundational role in shaping public cooperation, particularly in the context of digital government services where face-to-face interactions are limited and perceptions of risk are heightened (Alkraiji & Ameen, 2022; Chen et al., 2023). In the digital age, trust is increasingly influenced by citizens’ predisposition to trust, perceptions of technological reliability, and the reputation of governmental institutions (Fjaeran & Aven, 2021; Hooda et al., 2022). Trust in government extends beyond technological tools and reflects broader evaluations of institutional competence, transparency, responsiveness, and alignment with public values (Alzahrani et al., 2017). Studies reveal that satisfaction with digital services, including e-government platforms, directly influences trust, as citizens interpret service quality as indicative of government intent and capacity (Nawafleh, 2020; Alsarraf et al., 2022; Li & Shang, 2023). Research consistently confirms a positive association between trust in government and citizen satisfaction, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Alhefaity et al. (2026) 4 where higher trust levels are linked to increased confidence, engagement, and perception of public service value (Janssen et al., 2018; Kang & Zhu, 2021; Chan et al., 2023). In addition, the multidimensional nature of trust (encompassing competence, benevolence, and honesty) emerges through evaluations of government communication, digital responsiveness, and the ethical use of technologies (Porumbescu, 2016; Porumbescu et al., 2021; Ingrams et al., 2022). However, this process is sensitive to citizens’ subjective experiences, societal conditions, and governance transparency (Fawzi et al., 2021; Mansoor, 2021). In the context of the UAE, where AI is increasingly central to public service delivery, ensuring citizen trust in the government is essential for successful technology adoption and long-term satisfaction (Qin & Li, 2024). Citizens’ perceptions of ethical AI use, fairness in digital governance, and institutional accountability are key determinants of satisfaction in AI- enabled environments (Hooda et al., 2022; AlAwadhi et al., 2023). As the UAE continues its smart governance transformation, fostering trust in the government (particularly in law enforcement) is critical to reinforcing public confidence, service uptake, and societal cohesion. On the basis of this synthesis, the following hypothesis is proposed: H3: Trust in the government significantly affects citizen satisfaction. 2.4. Citizen Satisfaction Citizen satisfaction represents a critical benchmark for evaluating the performance and legitimacy of government services. In the context of public administration, it is generally defined as the degree to which citizens' expectations regarding service quality, efficiency, and fairness are met or exceeded (Mosimanegape, 2020). This satisfaction is shaped not only by the technical delivery of services but also by citizens’ emotional and cognitive evaluations of their service experiences (Bastiaansen, 2019; Chan et al., 2021). Factors such as accessibility, responsiveness, transparency, and the perceived competence of public institutions are central to shaping satisfaction levels (Porumbescu, 2017; Lamsal & Gupta, 2022). Within the domain of e-government and digital public services, citizen satisfaction has additional dimensions. It reflects citizen judgments about the usability, reliability, and perceived benefits of digital interactions with government systems (Alkraiji & Ameen, 2022). Especially in smart governance contexts such as the UAE, where AI technologies are integrated into service delivery, citizen satisfaction is not only a reflection of technical performance but also a measure of digital trust and inclusivity (Kumagai & Ilorio, 2020). A successful e-government system must, therefore, balance functional outcomes with positive emotional experiences to foster sustained citizen engagement and trust in government. In the realm of policing services, citizen satisfaction becomes an even more complex construct. It is influenced not only by service quality but also by perceptions of safety, procedural justice, and the ethical use of surveillance technologies (Nor et al., 2021; Merenda et al., 2021). Studies have shown that satisfaction is heightened when police services are delivered with transparency, timeliness, and professionalism qualities increasingly supported by AI technologies (Chatterjee et al., 2022; Ekaabi, 2020). For example, AI-enabled systems such as predictive analytics, real-time crime detection, and automated reporting platforms have contributed to shorter response times, reduced crime-related uncertainty, and streamlined citizen‒ police interactions, all of which significantly increase satisfaction (Radwan et al., 2023; Kulal et al., 2024). However, research also warns of emerging challenges. Concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, and opaque decision-making processes inherent in many AI applications can undermine public confidence, particularly in sensitive domains such as law enforcement (Song et al., 2022; Bagaric et al., 2022). When AI systems are perceived as intrusive or ethically ambiguous, satisfaction may decline, regardless of gains in efficiency. Hence, it is crucial that AI adoption in policing not only improves operational performance but also aligns with citizens’ values and expectations regarding fairness and human oversight (Brill et al., 2022; Agrawal, 2024). Empirical evidence further reinforces the link between citizen satisfaction and trust in government institutions (Garritzmann et al., 2023). Satisfied citizens are more likely to exhibit trust, cooperate with public policies, and maintain long- term engagement with governmental initiatives (Li & Shang, 2023). Conversely, dissatisfaction (especially in contexts involving AI) can lead to mistrust, reduced service uptake, and diminished government credibility. This dynamic is particularly salient in the UAE, where AI plays a prominent role in public sector reform and where achieving global benchmarks in safety and citizen happiness is a national priority (UAE Government, 2023). In summary, citizen satisfaction in AI-supported policing environments must be understood as a multidimensional construct. It encompasses both instrumental factors (such as speed, accuracy, and service delivery efficiency) and affective dimensions, such as emotional reassurance, perceived fairness, and ethical integrity. For governments such as the UAE, which are at the forefront of smart policing, prioritizing citizen satisfaction is not only about improving service performance but also about building a sustainable, trust-based relationship with the public. In this context, satisfaction serves as both a goal and a gauge for effective, ethical, and inclusive digital governance. 2.5. Underpinning Theories To comprehensively explain how artificial intelligence influences citizen satisfaction in UAE policing services, this study draws upon an integrated framework that combines public value theory (PVT), expectation-confirmation theory (ECT), and IT assimilation theory. These three theories offer distinct yet interrelated lenses to capture the multidimensional nature of citizen https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Alhefaity et al. (2026) 5 engagement with AI-enabled public services. PVT, pioneered by Moore (1997), focuses on the legitimacy, transparency, and responsiveness of public institutions in creating value for society. In the context of policing, PVT underscores that technological advancement (such as AI implementation) is valuable only when it aligns with societal expectations of fairness, accountability, and safety (Bryson et al., 2014; Torfing et al., 2021). PVT is particularly salient in evaluating whether AI technologies reinforce or erode the public legitimacy of law enforcement agencies in high-stakes governance environments such as the UAE. ECT, which was originally formulated by Oliver (2014) and adapted in public management contexts, provides a psychological mechanism for understanding how satisfaction emerges. ECT posits that satisfaction results from the comparison between citizens’ preservice expectations and their actual experiences. In AI-driven public services, this theory explains how citizens evaluate the quality, fairness, and usefulness of digital policing tools (such as predictive analytics and automated service delivery) against what they anticipate (Bhattacherjee, 2001; AlSokkar et al., 2024). When services exceed or meet expectations, satisfaction increases; if they fall short, dissatisfaction or mistrust may emerge. Thus, ECT is crucial for analyzing perception-based judgments of the acceptance and success of AI in public service. In contrast, IT assimilation theory provides an organizational and structural perspective, focusing on how deeply new technologies are embedded into routine public service processes. Rather than examining citizen perception or legitimacy alone, this theory addresses the degree to which AI systems are institutionalized within policing operations, both in terms of breadth (across services such as surveillance, traffic control, or administrative systems) and depth (in decision-making, strategic planning, and communication) (De Mattos & Laurindo, 2017; Chatterjee et al., 2020). The theory helps assess whether AI tools are merely adopted symbolically or truly assimilated to drive operational effectiveness and innovation in the public sector. The interplay among these three theories allows for a multidimensional understanding of AI implementation in public policing. Specifically, while ECT addresses perceptual alignment between citizen expectations and actual AI-driven service experiences, the PVT emphasizes normative legitimacy, ensuring that AI adoption enhances trust, fairness, and the perceived social value of public services, and IT assimilation theory explains operational embedding, assessing whether AI is fully integrated into law enforcement routines rather than being treated as a superficial enhancement. Together, these frameworks create a cohesive analytical model that captures the subjective (citizen perception), normative (institutional legitimacy), and structural (organizational integration) dimensions of AI use in public policing. This triangulated perspective is particularly relevant in the UAE context, where digital transformation is rapid and where citizen trust is a cornerstone of national development strategies. By leveraging this theoretical synergy, the current research not only explains how AI affects citizen satisfaction but also offers deeper insights into how governments can align technological innovation with public value creation, institutional trust, and long-term service engagement. 2.6. Materials and methods Using a quantitative methodology, this study adopted a structured questionnaire to collect data in a cross-sectional manner. Given the study’s focus on evaluating the relationships among AI implementation, perceptions of public services, trust in the government, and citizen satisfaction within the Abu Dhabi Police, the chosen respondents were police officers and administrative personnel actively involved in or impacted by AI-related services. These participants were deemed most suitable, as they possess direct experience with AI tools and can provide reliable insights into service performance, technology engagement, and trust in public institutions. The population for this study was drawn from the Abu Dhabi Police, which comprises over 35,000 employees (Alkaabi et al., 2024) across various departments. Following the Krejcie and Morgan (1970) sample size table, a minimum of 380 participants was required to achieve statistical validity with a 95% confidence level. To accommodate nonresponses, the sample was increased to 500 respondents. The sample was selected via purposive sampling, which targeted three key units: AI-enhanced, operational, and administrative units. This approach ensures the inclusion of participants with relevant experience and exposure to AI technologies in policing. The questionnaire design followed a multistep process to ensure content validity and reliability. The instrument was developed in English and subjected to expert review, followed by a pilot test to assess its clarity and relevance. Reliability was confirmed through Cronbach’s alpha, and only items meeting reliability thresholds were retained. The final questionnaire included 35 items divided into five sections: demographic information and AI implementation (8 items) adapted from Chatterjee et al. (2022), Li et al. (2017), Liang et al. (2019). Perception of public services (8 items) adapted from Chatterjee et al. (2022); Valle-Cruz et al. (2020); Zuiderwijk et al. (2021); trust in government (5 items) adapted from Radwan et al. (2023), and citizen satisfaction (7 items) Chatterjee et al. (2022); Chatterjee (2019); Chohan et al. (2021); Zuiderwijk et al. (2021). All the constructs were measured via a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), a scale widely validated in public service and technology adoption research (Taherdoost, 2019; Sekaran & Bougie, 2016). Primary data collection was carried out electronically via official Abu Dhabi Police internal communication systems, including email and secure messaging platforms. The participants received an introductory note explaining the research purpose and assuring them of confidentiality and voluntary participation. A four- week data collection window allowed sufficient time for completion, and reminder notifications were sent to improve response rates. This process ensured the collection of high-quality, context-specific data. For data analysis, partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed via SmartPLS 3.3.9 software. PLS-SEM was selected because of its robustness in handling complex models, flexibility with small to medium sample sizes, and suitability for predictive research objectives (Hair et al., 2020). The analysis was conducted in two stages: (1) the measurement model assessment, which focused on construct reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity; and (2) the structural model assessment, which examined path coefficients, effect sizes (ƒ²), and R-squared values. Bootstrapping procedures with 5,000 resamples were used to test the significance of relationships and validate the proposed hypotheses. This comprehensive methodological framework ensures that the findings are not only statistically sound but also practically relevant to understanding the influence of AI technologies in enhancing public trust and satisfaction within the policing sector of the UAE. 4. Results The data for this research were collected by distributing 500 questionnaires to employees of the Abu Dhabi Police, specifically those in AI-enhanced units, operational units, and administrative and support units. Among the distributed questionnaires, 388 were returned, resulting in a response rate of 77.6%. Among these 388 questionnaires, 23 were incomplete or had missing values. Consequently, 23 questionnaires were excluded from the analysis, leaving a total of 365 valid questionnaires for statistical data analysis. Importantly, normality checks were not conducted on the finalized data, as SmartPLS does not require data to be normally distributed for statistical analysis (Hair et al., 2022). The survey was conducted from early January to the end of May 2024, and statistical analysis was used to identify errors in all the constructs during the data-gathering period. 4.1. The Measurement Model: Outer Model Evaluating the loading score of each item in its variable is critical to ensure that the variable receives proper and adequate loading from its associated factors. Any loading score equal to or greater than 0.708 is considered a proper loading. Any loading less than 0.4 is considered weak, and the item is removed. Any factor with a loading score between 0.4 and 0.708 can be retained or deleted on the basis of the analysis judgment (Hair et al., 2020). Therefore, factor loadings, composite reliability (CR), and average variance extracted (AVE) were used to assess the convergent validity of the measurement model, as recommended by Hair et al. (2022). The indicator outer loadings (Table 3 and Figure 2) confirm construct reliability, with most indicators exceeding the 0.708 threshold. Items falling below were removed, resulting in six valid indicators for AI implementation, five for the perception of public services, six for trust in government, and five for citizen satisfaction. The composite reliability and Cronbach's alpha (Table 3) for all the constructs exceeded 0.7, and the AVE values ranged from 0.631 to 0.724, confirming convergent validity. Discriminant validity was confirmed through Fornell-Larcker (1981) (Table 4), ensuring that the constructs were distinct and accurately measured. The discriminant validity was calculated by taking the square root of the AVE across all factors. Discussion The findings of this study provide strong empirical support for the influence of AI implementation on citizen satisfaction with police services in Abu Dhabi. AI technologies such as predictive analytics, real-time data processing, and automated service delivery tools have significantly improved operational efficiency and responsiveness. These findings align with prior research that has demonstrated how AI enhances public service performance and citizen trust by increasing transparency and reducing response times (Zhang et al., 2022; Kulal et al., 2024). Moreover, AI applications such as real-time crime tracking and automated traffic management are positively associated with citizen perceptions of fairness and accuracy in service delivery (Goh et al., 2020; Al Shamsi & Safei, 2023). As such, AI not only supports operational excellence but also strengthens public engagement by fostering transparency and service predictability (Ahn & Chen, 2022; Chatterjee et al., 2022). However, the positive impact of AI implementation is conditional upon how well these technologies are aligned with citizen expectations. When AI systems are designed with fairness, ethical integrity, and ease of use in mind, they contribute positively to satisfaction levels. Conversely, poor implementation (particularly in contexts that neglect transparency or accessibility) may erode trust and reduce citizen satisfaction (Liang et al., 2019). Equally important, this study confirms that perceptions of public service quality play a vital role in shaping citizen satisfaction. These findings are consistent with expectation‒confirmation theory, which asserts that satisfaction is contingent on how well service performance meets or exceeds prior expectations (He & Ma, 2021; Alkraiji & Ameen, 2022). In this context, citizen perceptions of police efficiency, accessibility, and reliability (further enhanced by AI systems) directly contribute to their overall satisfaction (Kulal et al., 2024; Henman, 2020). The integration of smart service platforms, interactive applications, and responsive digital interfaces by the UAE police has strengthened the perceived value of public services, thereby improving satisfaction levels (Almesafri & Habes, 2022). Moreover, the predictive and proactive capabilities of AI have reshaped how citizens evaluate the effectiveness of public services. Tools that support resource optimization and real-time responsiveness contribute to a sense of safety and reliability, both of which are critical to satisfaction (McDaniel & Pease, 2021; Zuiderwijk et al., 2021). Despite these advancements, concerns around data privacy, algorithmic fairness, and ethical transparency must be addressed to sustain high levels of trust and satisfaction (Wirtz et al., 2021; Kulal et al., 2024). Finally, the study validates the significance of trust in the government as a determinant of citizen satisfaction. Consistent with a wide body of literature, the results underscore that public trust in institutions (rooted in transparency, reliability, and ethical conduct) strongly influences how citizens perceive and respond to service delivery (Pérez- Morote et al., 2020; Janssen et al., 2018). Trust enables citizens to feel secure in their interactions with digital and AI-driven systems, especially in sectors such as policing, where service reliability and ethical behavior are paramount (Alzahrani et al., 2018; Chan et al., 2021). Studies show that when citizens believe in the capability and integrity of public institutions, they are more likely to engage with and endorse technological innovations (Santa et al., 2019; Porumbescu et al., 2022). The UAE’s commitment to building smart, secure, and citizen-oriented public service systems has laid the groundwork for these positive perceptions. Nevertheless, the long-term success of AI-driven governance depends on maintaining this trust through robust data protection, ethical AI governance, and citizen engagement strategies (Kim et al., 2022; Nawafleh, 2022). Overall, this research successfully meets its objectives by empirically demonstrating that AI implementation, service perception, and trust in government are all significant contributors to citizen satisfaction. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive understanding of how AI and trust dynamics shape public attitudes toward modern policing in the UAE. As digital transformation accelerates across the public sector, these insights offer valuable guidance for designing inclusive, ethical, and citizen-centric AI solutions that sustain public trust and satisfaction. 5.1. Contributions and Implications This research contributes both theoretically and practically to the growing body of knowledge on AI integration in public services, particularly within the context of law enforcement in the UAE. The findings not only confirm the significant role of AI implementation and public service perception in enhancing citizen satisfaction but also highlight the pivotal role of trust in the government as a foundational element in citizen–state interactions. The theoretical implications of this study lie in its contribution to extending the existing frameworks of public value theory (PVT) and expectation-confirmation theory (ECT) within the realm of AI-driven public services. Research confirms that https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Alhefaity et al. (2026) 11 AI implementation significantly influences citizen satisfaction by improving service delivery efficiency, responsiveness, and transparency (Zhang et al., 2022; Kulal et al., 2024). Moreover, it aligns with ECT by showing that positive perceptions of public services, when aligned with citizen expectations, lead to greater satisfaction (He & Ma, 2021; Alkraiji & Ameen, 2022). Research has also demonstrated that trust in the government plays a crucial role in shaping public perceptions of AI-enabled services, reinforcing the importance of trust in the government in public administration (Janssen et al., 2018; Alzahrani et al., 2018). By applying and extending these theories to a law enforcement context, particularly in a technologically advanced setting such as the UAE, this study offers a robust conceptual framework for understanding how public trust and satisfaction are influenced by AI integration. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for policymakers, law enforcement agencies, and technology developers. Policymakers can use these results to develop AI governance strategies that prioritize transparency, citizen engagement, and ethical AI usage. Law enforcement agencies, in particular, are encouraged to design AI systems that are citizen-centric, responsive, and transparent to maximize public trust and satisfaction (Chatterjee et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2019). For AI developers, the study underscores the need to design explainable and ethical AI tools that resonate with the public’s values and expectations. The UAE’s smart policing initiatives can benefit from these insights by focusing on AI applications that improve accessibility, speed, fairness, and security in service delivery. Additionally, the integration of feedback mechanisms and public communication strategies can further increase citizen satisfaction. 6. Conclusions This study sets out to examine the impact of AI implementation, perceptions of public services, and trust in government on citizen satisfaction with the Abu Dhabi Police. The analysis revealed that AI adoption plays a significant role in enhancing citizen satisfaction by improving service efficiency, responsiveness, and overall quality. Similarly, citizens’ perceptions of public service performance were found to have a strong positive influence on satisfaction, underlining the importance of delivering services that are reliable, transparent, and responsive to public needs. Trust in government emerged as both a direct determinant of satisfaction and a mediator between AI, public service perceptions, and satisfaction. This highlights that while technology and service quality are critical, their impact is maximized only when citizens trust that government institutions are acting competently and fairly. The findings demonstrate that citizen satisfaction is shaped by a combination of technological advancement, service performance, and institutional trust. In particular, the partial mediating effect of trust in government suggests that while AI and public service perceptions directly contribute to satisfaction, their influence is strengthened when citizens have confidence in government intentions and capabilities. This underlines the importance of building trust as a central pillar of AI-enabled governance. By achieving all four research objectives, the study contributes valuable insights into the dynamics of AI-driven public services in the UAE context. The results provide theoretical contributions by validating the roles of Public Value Theory, Expectation-Confirmation Theory, and IT Assimilation Theory in explaining citizen satisfaction with technology-enabled governance. Practically, the findings support the development of AI strategies that balance efficiency with transparency and emphasize trust-building as an essential outcome. Overall, this research concludes that the successful integration of AI in public services depends not only on technical performance but also on the government’s ability to foster trust and meet citizen expectations. These insights are particularly significant for the UAE as it advances toward its Vision 2031, highlighting how AI technologies, when strategically implemented, can contribute to safer communities, stronger governance, and higher levels of citizen satisfaction. JSON: Name: ai_trust_pls_sem_abu_dhabi Title: PLS-SEM analysis of the effect of AI implementation on citizen satisfaction in Abu Dhabi policing Short Hypothesis: Higher levels of AI implementation in Abu Dhabi police services cause increased citizen satisfaction, and this relationship is partially mediated by trust in government. Related Work: Prior work has applied structural equation modeling and survey-based methods to quantify relationships among technology adoption, perceived service quality, trust, and satisfaction in public-sector settings. Approaches differ in choice of respondents (citizens vs. public employees), model specification (direct effects only versus mediation/moderation), and analytical framework (PLS-SEM, covariance-based SEM, or regression). Existing studies commonly report positive associations between digital service quality and satisfaction and between trust and satisfaction, but limitations persist: many studies are cross-sectional and reliant on single-source self-reported data, reducing causal interpretability; few investigations combine objective service performance logs with perceptual measures; regional studies in the Gulf are sparse and often use small or nonrepresentative samples; mediation analyses are underpowered or incomplete; and model validation (predictive performance, measurement invariance across groups) is frequently omitted. Additionally, research rarely contrasts alternative SEM approaches or performs systematic ablation to quantify mediator contributions. Abstract: This research evaluates whether AI implementation in Abu Dhabi policing increases citizen satisfaction and quantifies the mediating role of trust in government. We propose a quantitative pipeline combining standardized survey instruments, administrative service-performance logs, and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to estimate direct and mediated paths among AI implementation, perception of public services, trust in government, and citizen satisfaction. The main contribution is a validated, predictive structural model that reports effect sizes, mediation estimates, and out-of-sample predictive metrics for the Abu Dhabi policing context. Expected outcomes include (1) estimated path coefficients with bootstrap confidence intervals, (2) quantified mediation by trust, (3) model predictive performance (R2, Q2, SRMR, PLSpredict), and (4) an ablation analysis that isolates the incremental explanatory power of AI signals versus perceptual mediators. Results will inform evidence-based governance choices by clarifying how technological deployment and institutional credibility jointly shape satisfaction. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary survey of Abu Dhabi residents (n_target=1000) sampled stratified by emirate district, age, gender, and service usage; instrument: validated Likert scales for AI implementation exposure (6 items), perception of public services (5 items), trust in government (6 items), and citizen satisfaction (5 items); control covariates: age, gender, education, frequency of police contact. (2) Secondary administrative logs from Abu Dhabi Police (if accessible) for the same period: response times, case clearance rates, complaint counts, and AI system usage frequency (aggregated per district, monthly for 12 months). Data preprocessing: remove incomplete responses (>20% missing), impute remaining missing via multiple imputation, assess common-method bias (Harman single-factor) and multicollinearity (VIF threshold 5). Baselines: (A) OLS regression models predicting satisfaction using AI implementation only; (B) covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) with same measurement model; (C) PLS-SEM without mediators; (D) PLS-SEM with perception mediator only; (E) PLS-SEM with trust mediator only; (F) Full PLS-SEM with both mediators (proposed). Evaluation metrics: measurement model: indicator loadings, Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, AVE, Fornell-Larcker; structural model: path coefficients (β), t-values, p-values (bootstrapping 5,000 resamples), R2 for endogenous constructs, effect sizes (ƒ2), predictive relevance (Q2), SRMR, and PLSpredict RMSE for out-of-sample predictive comparison. Experimental setup: estimate all models using SmartPLS or equivalent; perform multi-group analysis (MGA) by respondent subgroup (gender and high/low AI exposure) to test invariance; ablation study: compare ΔR2 and change in β for citizen satisfaction after removing trust mediator and after removing perception mediator; sensitivity analysis: rerun models using only administrative performance metrics as AI implementation proxy and compare coefficients to self-report AI measures. Report bootstrap CIs and Cohen's d for group contrasts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Dependence on cross-sectional survey data limits causal inference and temporal ordering of mediation; self-report measures introduce social desirability and common-method bias; sampling bias if resident survey does not reach digitally marginalised or non-responders; restricted access to administrative logs or incomplete/aggregated logs can prevent linking objective performance to perceptions; measurement error in latent constructs may attenuate path estimates; small to moderate effect sizes may require larger samples for stable mediation estimates; cultural and institutional specificity of Abu Dhabi policing limits external generalizability to other jurisdictions; model misspecification (omitted confounders) can bias mediation estimates; multicollinearity among predictors can inflate variances and obscure individual effects; legal, ethical, and privacy constraints may limit data granularity and longitudinal follow-up.
